body_markdown:
Some recent advancements in headlight technology available in global markets could finally come to the United States, and the dated rules that have held back lighting technology and design are going to get a second look. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has begun updating its lighting standards.


The agency explains that the update is long overdue, and it plans to consult industry stakeholders (including car manufacturers), safety advocates, and technical experts to change the regulations. The government’s stated goals are to address headlight glare, modernize lighting technology, improve the performance of headlights, and streamline the testing procedures, presumably to make the homologation process easier. Interestingly, the NHTSA also wants to align U.S. regulations with international standards.


It’s too early to tell how headlight regulations will change. The first part of the process involves appointing up to 18 industry stakeholders to the panel that will analyze the current regulations and suggest areas of improvement. The NHTSA is letting members of the general public submit comments and nominate stakeholders via[a dedicated website](https://www.regulations.gov/) until November 9, 2026. How long the evaluation will take hasn’t been announced yet, but the NHTSA wrote that it wants to accelerate the rule-making process.

One of the topics likely to come up during the discussions is the legality of adaptive-beam headlights, which are sometimes called matrix lights (or matrix beams; shown above) in marketing-speak. Odds are your daily driver has two headlight settings: High beams and low beams. In contrast, the matrix lights consist of numerous LED elements that can be individually dimmed or turned off to avoid blinding oncoming cars. The matrix system relies on an armada of sensors to know which lighting elements it needs to dim and which ones can stay bright. There’s no high-beam or low-beam setting with matrix lights; it’s pretty much a mix of both.


This technology has been legal in the United States since 2022, but American standards differ from European standards. It’s easier and cheaper for carmakers to deactivate this feature using software than to develop matrix beams specifically for the United States. Updating headlight regulations in the United States and aligning them with international standards could give American-market models the same headlights as their European counterparts while encouraging more carmakers to invest in better lighting tech.
